reason: A thallus (liverwort, hornwort, lichen) can be shiny; the examples fit.
Ellipsoid and globose are 3-D shapes of berries.

Bracts can be wide, but most examples are measurements ('1-2 mm wide'), which are width values, not 'increased width'. A rule would send numeric measures to width and keep only comparative words (wide, broad) here.
Lance-ovate is a normal bract shape.
Involucral bracts (phyllaries) can be keeled. The 'not keeled' examples need negation handling.
Pedicels can be sticky (viscid), often with glands.
Leaf lobes can be broad.
A perigynium (Carex) can be glossy or shiny.
Thickened or thick perigynia occur. The 'stout' stipe-like base example is a different part, so the rule must read the part word.
A corolla can be large or enlarged. Examples like 'lower lip enlarged' refer to a sub-part, so check the part word.
Boat-shaped (navicular) petals are scaphoid.
Fruit pulp colour is meaningful, and 'pulp' is mapped to fruit storage parenchyma.
Knotty or nodose rhizomes are knobbled.
Pendulous ovules hang down, which is what drooping means here.
A viscidium (orchid) can be orbicular. 'Suborbiculate' is close enough.
Pale seeds are pale in colour. Examples about ribs, skin or margin are sub-parts, so check the part word.

Frond texture (leathery, papery) is fine. The examples also include 'flat' (a shape) and 'subglabrous or with stellate scales' (indumentum). A rule would allow only texture words (leathery, papery, herbaceous, membranous).
Scales or trichomes on a stem can be appressed or spreading, which is position or orientation.
Sepals can be twisted.
A perianth can be spreading. Examples about lobes or tips are sub-parts, so check the part word.
A pruinose (waxy bloom) stem is glaucous in the sense used for these terms.
An anther cap (orchid) has a colour.
'Solitary' or 'paired' racemes describe how they are arranged, which is spatial pattern.
Secondary veins can be slender.
A geniculate (bent, knee-like) stem base is bent.
An entire margin is a standard quality. The bearer is a margin class, so this is fine.
Leaf lobes can be emarginate (notched at the tip).
The examples are measurements ('column 4-5 mm long'), which are length values, not 'increased length'. This pair comes from a wrong reading, and length should be used.
Sori can be large.
Axes such as rachises can be pubescent.
A pistil can be short or shorter than other parts. Comparative statements need a comparison rule, but the pair is meaningful.
Fruit stalks can be thickened.
Utricles (Carex) are often inflated.
Petals can be undivided (entire) or divided.
Archegonia have a length (bryophytes).
Sporangia can be kidney-shaped (reniform).
Counting vessels per bundle is an amount, and the examples are correct.
Rudimentary pedicels are vestigial. The 'peduncle' example is a different part, so check the part word.
An apex has a shape (obtuse, acuminate, mucronate). Examples like 'apex with mucro' or 'mucro 0.1 mm' describe a separate structure. A rule would split shape words from 'with X' structures.
A leaf lamina can be translucent.
Imbricate and valvate describe how calyx lobes are arranged (aestivation), which is spatial pattern.
Capsules can be elongated ('longer than wide').
Pale petals are low in colour saturation.
Seeds can be subovoid.
Calyx parts can be hairy. Examples such as 'lobes 6-9, hairy' include a count, so check the part word.
A pyriform (pear-shaped) ovary is a standard description.

The examples are about leaf veins standing out on the surface, not the inner vascular bundle. Prominence is fine for veins, but the bearer may be a wrong mapping. A rule would map 'vein' to leaf vein classes and not to vascular bundle.
Petals can be woolly (lanate).
A pulvinus (geniculum) has a length.
An ellipsoid calyx is prolate. Prolate is a slightly narrower term than ellipsoid, but it is acceptable here.
Leaflets or leaflet margins can be reflexed. Examples about 'pinnae' are fern parts, so check the part word.
A saccate (sac-like) orchid hypochile is a concave 3-D shape.
Cymes have a length.
Spinulose achenes bear small spines.
The examples are French ('arrondies', 'nervure') and seem to describe leaflet or vein ends, not the legume. A rule would need the real bearer of 'obtuse'.
Secretory tissue (glands) can be inconspicuous.
A petiole can be twisted.
Bud scales have a 2-D shape (ovate, etc.).
'Characteristic' is a very generic root term. The examples are alternatives ('smooth or reticulate', 'entire or lobed') that need more specific qualities.
A tooth can be present or absent on a leaf lamina or phyllome.
